Interactive checking

Reference

Watch out — every time
  • Same units top and bottom. τ = amount ÷ flux only works if both describe the same thing in the same units: mol and mol/yr, or m³ and m³/yr.
  • Volumes: 1 km³ = 10⁹ m³ = 10¹² L;  1 m³ = 1000 L;  1 mm of water over 1 m² = 1 L.
  • Concentrations: 1 mmol/L = 10⁻³ mol/L;  1 µmol/L = 10⁻⁶ mol/L.
  • The Darcy flux q is not the speed water moves. Water only travels through the pores: v = q / nₑ.
  • Time: 1 year = 365.25 days = 3.156 × 10⁷ s.
  • K: 1 m/s = 86 400 m/day (the slides use m/s, this practical m/day).
Powers-of-ten toolbox
10³ × 10⁴ = 10⁷multiplying → add the exponents
10⁹ ÷ 10³ = 10⁶dividing → subtract the exponents
1.332 × 10⁹ km³ × 10¹² L/km³ = 1.332 × 10²¹ Lunits cancel like numbers
0.33 mmol/L = 0.33 × 10⁻³ = 3.3 × 10⁻⁴ mol/Lmove the decimal point, adjust the exponent

Calculator: type 1.332 × 10⁹ as 1.332 EXP 9 (or ×10ˣ), not 1.332 × 10 ^ 9 — that's easy to mistype.

TermMeaning
Residence time τAverage time something spends in a reservoir: τ = amount stored ÷ flux (at steady state, flux in = flux out).
Area-normalised rateA flux divided by the area it crosses, as a depth per time (mm/yr, m/day). Lets you compare rain, runoff, recharge, evaporation and groundwater flow directly.
Hydraulic conductivity KHow easily water flows through a material (m/day): from ~10⁻⁷ for clay to ~10³ for gravel.
Darcy flux qVolume of water crossing 1 m² of aquifer per day (m³ per m² per day = m/day). Not the speed of the water.
Effective porosity nₑFraction of the rock made of connected pores that water can flow through.
Retardation factor RHow many times slower a sorbing contaminant moves than the groundwater (R = 1: moves with the water).
CatchmentAll the land that drains to one outlet point. Its boundary (the divide) follows ridges.
Solute yieldFlux of a dissolved substance leaving a catchment ÷ catchment area (mol or t per km² per year) = runoff × concentration.
C–Q relationshipHow a solute's concentration changes with discharge: dilution (falls), chemostasis (nearly constant), mobilisation (rises).
Discharge vs runoffDischarge Q = volume per time (m³/s). Runoff = discharge ÷ catchment area, as a depth per time (mm/yr).
Power law, C = a·QbOn log–log axes it is a straight line: log C = log a + b · log Q. The slope b says how concentration responds to flow.
Part 1

Soil and groundwater — how fast does groundwater, and a contaminant, reach a stream?

Starts after Block 1 (soil and groundwater) | ⏱ 25 min
Darcy flux:   q = K · Δh / L    (K = hydraulic conductivity; Δh = head difference; L = distance; Δh/L = hydraulic gradient)(1)
Discharge:   Q = q · A      Water speed:   v = q / nₑ      Travel time:   t = distance / v      Sorbing contaminant:   t × R(2)
Worked example: A gravel aquifer under a river terrace

K = 100 m/day; the water table drops 2 m over 400 m; effective porosity 0.25. How long does water take to travel 1 km?

  1. Gradient: Δh / L = 2 m ÷ 400 m = 0.005.
  2. Darcy flux: q = 100 m/day × 0.005 = 0.5 m/day.
  3. Water speed: v = 0.5 ÷ 0.25 = 2 m/day.
  4. Travel time: 1000 m ÷ 2 m/day = 500 days ≈ 1.4 years.

Explore: how much does the rock matter?

explore
Slide K from clay (left) to gravel (right). How long would groundwater take to travel 1 km?
Darcy flux q = – m/day
water speed v = – m/day
time to travel 1 km = – years

How fast does groundwater reach the stream?

⏱ 20 min
A homogeneous sand aquifer, 10 m thick and 100 m wide. Well A: hydraulic head 50 m; well B, 500 m down-gradient: 45 m. The stream is 1 km from well A. Effective porosity nₑ = 0.30. Steady state.
1a)
What is the hydraulic gradient between A and B?
💡 Gradient = head difference ÷ distance.
💡 (50 − 45) m ÷ 500 m
Worked solution

Answer: 0.01 (= 1%)

(50 − 45) m ÷ 500 m = 0.01 (no units).
1b)
Choose a K for sand from the conductivity table (m/day). Any value in the sand range works — the next answers are checked against your choice.
m/day
💡 Sand: 1–10² m/day. 10 m/day is a sensible middle value.
Worked solution
Sand: 1–100 m/day; 10 m/day is a sensible middle value.
1c)
What is the Darcy flux q (m/day)?
m/day
💡 Eq. 1: q = K × gradient.
Worked solution

Answer: K × 0.01 (0.1 m/day for K = 10)

q = 10 m/day × 0.01 = 0.1 m/day for K = 10 (range 0.01–1 m/day).
1d)
How much water flows through the aquifer each day, Q (m³/day)?
m³/day
💡 Q = q × A, where A is the cross-section the water flows through.
💡 A = thickness × width = 10 m × 100 m.
Worked solution

Answer: q × 1000 m² (100 m³/day for K = 10)

Q = 0.1 m/day × 1000 m² = 100 m³/day for K = 10 (range 10–1000).
1e)
How fast does the water actually move (m/day)?
m/day
💡 Eq. 2: v = q / nₑ.
💡 Look at the figure above: only the pores carry the water.
Worked solution

Answer: q ÷ 0.30 (0.33 m/day for K = 10)

v = 0.1 ÷ 0.30 = 0.33 m/day for K = 10: 3.3 × faster than q.
1f)
How long does water from well A take to reach the stream (years)?
years
💡 t = distance ÷ v; 1 km = 1000 m.
💡 Days → years: ÷ 365.25.
Worked solution

Answer: 8.2 years for K = 10

t = 1000 m ÷ 0.33 m/day = 3000 days = 8.2 years for K = 10 (range 0.8–82 years).
1g)
A spill at well A releases nitrate (moves with the water) and a pesticide that sorbs onto grains (R = 5). How long until the pesticide reaches the stream (years)?
years
💡 Nitrate arrives with the water: your answer to 1f.
💡 R = 5 means it moves 5 times slower, so it takes 5 times longer.
Worked solution

Answer: 5 × your answer to 1f (41 years for K = 10)

Nitrate: 8.2 years (K = 10). Pesticide: 5 × 8.2 ≈ 41 years. The same spill gives the stream a nitrate pulse first and a pesticide problem decades later.

1h. Bonus: is the landfill liner good enough?

⏱ 10 minbonus
A landfill sits on a 5 m thick clay layer above the aquifer. Clay: K = 10⁻⁴ m/day, porosity 0.4. Leachate seeps straight down, with a hydraulic gradient of 1.
a)
How long does leachate take to cross the clay (years)?
years
💡 The same steps as 1c–1f: q = K × gradient, v = q / porosity, t = thickness ÷ v.
Worked solution

Answer: 54.8 years

q = 10⁻⁴ m/day; v = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ m/day; t = 5 m ÷ 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ m/day = 20 000 days ≈ 55 years.
b)
Is that 'safe'? What could make it much faster in reality?
💡 Think about cracks, and about what happens to clay when it dries.
Model answer
Decades is slow, but landfills last longer than that. Cracks, root holes, sand lenses or a damaged liner make preferential pathways with K many orders of magnitude higher, cutting the travel time to months or less. Hence engineered liners and monitoring wells.
✋
End of Part 1. Wait for Block 2. Finished early? Try bonus 1h, or play with the sliders.
Part 2

Catchments and rivers — the River Wear above Burnhope, and river chemistry

Starts after Block 2 (catchments and rivers) | ⏱ 30 min

Two tasks. A: find the catchment of the River Wear at the Burnhope gauge and work out its water balance. B: use real river data to measure how two dissolved substances respond to flow.

Task A: the Burnhope catchment

  1. Read the land. Find the ★ gauge below the dam, the reservoir, and Burnhope Burn flowing in from the west. Water reaches the gauge only if it gets into this stream network. On a contour map a ridge is where contours bend into V or U shapes pointing downhill; a valley is where they point uphill.
  2. Test with raindrops. In Raindrop mode, click at least six places: three you think drain to the ★ and three you think don't (try north of the northern ridge, towards Killhope Burn).
  3. Draw the boundary. Switch to Draw boundary. Start at the ★, walk uphill crossing contours at right angles, follow the ridge crests all the way round, never cross a stream, and come back to the ★. Click to add points (20–40 is plenty), then press Check my boundary. Try once properly before you press Show the true catchment.
Raindrop mode: click anywhere on the map to see where the water goes.
raindrop pathyour boundary inside bothcatchment you missedyour extra (drains elsewhere)

Real topography (Terrarium elevation tiles, ~11 m), contours every 10 m (bold every 50 m), streams draining more than 0.3 km², British National Grid 1 km squares (labels in km, square NY). The red ★ is the Environment Agency gauge below Burnhope Reservoir (NRFA station 24011). Flow routing: steepest descent on a 22 m grid, so the true boundary is stepped.

Catchment water balance:   dS/dt = P − Q − ET    (dS/dt = change in storage over time; as depths per year over the catchment; over a year dS/dt ≈ 0)(3)

The catchment and its water balance

⏱ 15 min
For 1991–2020 the catchment above the gauge received on average P = 1530 mm of rain a year, and the mean flow at the gauge was Q = 0.582 m³/s (UKCEH National River Flow Archive).
2a)
What is the area of the catchment above the gauge (km²)? Use your boundary on the map (or, on paper, count the 1 km squares inside it).
km²
💡 Start at the ★, go uphill at right angles to the contours, follow the ridges and close the loop.
💡 'Check my boundary' gives your area; 'Show the true catchment' gives the answer.
Worked solution

Answer: ≈ 20 km²

The true catchment is 20.2 km² (NRFA: 20.5 km²). A careful square count lands within 10–15 %.
2b)
Express the mean flow as runoff: a depth of water per year over the catchment (mm/yr). Use 20.2 km².
mm/yr
💡 Volume per year = 0.582 m³/s × 3.156 × 10⁷ s.
💡 Depth = volume ÷ area (m²), then m → mm.
Worked solution

Answer: 908 mm/yr

0.582 × 3.156 × 10⁷ = 1.84 × 10⁷ m³/yr; ÷ 20.2 × 10⁶ m² = 0.908 m = 908 mm/yr.
2c)
Over a year the stored water hardly changes. How much water leaves the catchment in other ways (mm/yr)?
mm/yr
💡 Eq. 3 with dS/dt = 0: P − Q = what is left.
Worked solution

Answer: 622 mm/yr

1530 − 908 ≈ 622 mm/yr.
2d)
Evapotranspiration from cold, wet Pennine moorland is only about 350–450 mm/yr. What else most likely takes water out before the gauge?
Worked solution

Answer: water piped out of the reservoir for public supply

Burnhope is a water-supply reservoir: water is piped out for public supply, and only a fixed compensation flow plus any spill passes the gauge. The catchment is not natural — which matters for its chemistry too.

Task B: river chemistry, concentration and discharge

Sagehen Creek drains about 27 km² of forested volcanic and granitic rock in the Sierra Nevada, California; most of its water arrives as spring snowmelt. The US Geological Survey sampled it about once a month from 2001 to 2018: each point below is one water sample, plotted against the discharge when it was taken. A concentration–discharge (C–Q) relationship is often a power law, C = a·Qb. Taking logs, log C = log a + b·log Q: on log–log axes it becomes a straight line with slope b. Compare the two solutes on linear axes and on log–log axes.

Sagehen Creek near Truckee, California (346 samples, 2001–2018)

How do calcium and DOC respond to flow?

⏱ 12 min
Copy the table into Excel (or download the CSV) to answer 2e and 2f.
2e)
Fit a straight line to log₁₀(Ca) against log₁₀(Q). What is the slope b for calcium?
💡 Make two new columns with =LOG10(…) of Q and of Ca, and plot them as an XY scatter.
💡 The slope of that line is b: =SLOPE(log Ca cells, log Q cells), or a linear trendline with its equation shown.
Worked solution

Answer: b ≈ −0.33

b = −0.33 (R² = 0.93). Calcium falls as flow rises, but far more gently than simple dilution (b = −1): at ten times the flow it is 10−0.33 ≈ 0.46× as concentrated, not 0.1×.
2f)
Do the same for DOC. What is b?
💡 Same steps, with a =LOG10() column for DOC.
Worked solution

Answer: b ≈ +0.36

b = +0.36 (R² = 0.47): DOC rises with flow. The scatter is larger: DOC also depends on the season and on how much organic matter has built up in the soil since the last flush.
2g)
Which describes Sagehen Creek?
Worked solution

Answer: calcium is diluted, though much less than simple dilution; DOC is mobilised

Calcium: b ≈ −⅓, between chemostatic (0) and simple dilution (−1). DOC: b > 0, mobilisation (flushing).
2h)
Why do the two solutes respond to flow in opposite ways? Think about where in the catchment each one comes from, and which flow paths carry the water at low and at high flow.
💡 Where is calcium released, and where is organic carbon produced?
💡 When the snow melts, the water table rises. Which layers does the water then flow through?
Model answer
Calcium comes from mineral weathering, so it is highest in water that has been in contact with rock for a long time: the deeper groundwater that feeds the stream at low flow. During snowmelt, extra water reaches the stream through shallow soil and near-surface paths with little time to react, so calcium is diluted — but only weakly, because weathering keeps supplying it (close to chemostasis). DOC is made in the organic-rich topsoil: when the water table rises into those layers, the flow flushes DOC into the stream. The sign of b reflects whether a solute is richer in shallow water (b > 0) or in deep water (b < 0).
✋
End of the practical. Finished early? Try the Bonus part: the ocean as one box. Or test more raindrops on the map: where does each one end up?
Bonus

The ocean as one box: how long does calcium stay?

If you finish Part 2 early, or at home | ⏱ 20 min
From water to chemistry: the same box for solutes
Measure a concentration C and every water budget becomes a chemical budget: amount = volume × C and flux = water flux × C. So τsolute = (volume × Creservoir) ÷ (water flux × Cinput). A solute that leaves easily (or reacts) has a short τ; one that stays behind when the water leaves has a long τ.
Steady state:   τ = amount in the reservoir ÷ flux through it    (both for the same substance, in matching units)(4)
Worked example: How long does a water molecule stay in the atmosphere?

Atmosphere: 12.7 × 10³ km³ of water. Global precipitation (the flux out): 486 × 10³ km³/yr.

  1. Both are in km³, so no conversion is needed: τ = 12.7 × 10³ ÷ 486 × 10³ = 0.0261 yr.
  2. In days: 0.0261 × 365.25 = 9.5 days. The rain falling today evaporated about a week and a half ago.

How long does calcium stay in the ocean?

⏱ 15 min
Rivers bring dissolved Ca²⁺ to the ocean. It leaves when corals, shellfish and plankton build calcium carbonate (CaCO₃) skeletons and shells that end up buried in seafloor sediment. Over thousands of years the two fluxes balance, so ocean calcium is close to steady state.
Data: river Ca²⁺ = 0.33 mmol/L;  global river discharge = 37 000 km³/yr;  ocean Ca²⁺ = 10.3 mmol/L;  ocean volume = 1.332 × 10⁹ km³.
a)
What is the ocean volume in litres?
L
💡 1 km³ = 10¹² L (see the watch-out box).
💡 1.332 × 10⁹ × 10¹² = ? (multiplying → add the exponents)
Worked solution

Answer: 1.33×1021 L

1.332 × 10⁹ km³ × 10¹² L/km³ = 1.332 × 10²¹ L.
b)
How many moles of Ca²⁺ are in the ocean?
mol
💡 Amount = volume (L) × concentration (mol/L).
💡 10.3 mmol/L = 1.03 × 10⁻² mol/L.
Worked solution

Answer: 1.37×1019 mol

1.332 × 10²¹ L × 1.03 × 10⁻² mol/L = 1.37 × 10¹⁹ mol.
c)
What is the river flux of Ca²⁺ into the ocean (mol/yr)?
mol/yr
💡 Flux = water flux (L/yr) × concentration (mol/L).
💡 37 000 km³/yr = 3.7 × 10¹⁶ L/yr; 0.33 mmol/L = 3.3 × 10⁻⁴ mol/L.
Worked solution

Answer: 1.22×1013 mol/yr

3.7 × 10¹⁶ L/yr × 3.3 × 10⁻⁴ mol/L = 1.22 × 10¹³ mol/yr.
d)
What is the residence time of Ca²⁺ in the ocean (million years)?
Myr
💡 τ = amount ÷ flux (Eq. 4).
💡 mol ÷ (mol/yr) = years. Then ÷ 10⁶ for million years.
Worked solution

Answer: 1.12 Myr

τ = 1.37 × 10¹⁹ ÷ 1.22 × 10¹³ = 1.12 × 10⁶ yr ≈ 1.1 Myr.
e)
Why does calcium stay in the ocean so much longer than water itself (about 3000 years)?
💡 How does water leave the ocean? Can calcium leave the same way?
Model answer
Water leaves easily, by evaporation, but calcium stays behind. Calcium only leaves when organisms lock it into CaCO₃ shells and skeletons that are buried, and that sink is slow compared with the huge amount of calcium already in the ocean.

One more: the ocean as an area-normalised rate

⏱ 5 minbonus
413 × 10³ km³ of water evaporates from the ocean each year. The ocean covers 3.61 × 10⁸ km².
What depth of water evaporates from the ocean each year (m/yr)?
m/yr
💡 Depth = volume ÷ area: km³ ÷ km² = km.
💡 Then km → m (× 1000).
Worked solution

Answer: 1.14 m/yr

413 × 10³ ÷ 3.61 × 10⁸ = 1.14 × 10⁻³ km/yr = 1.14 m/yr, about the same as the UK's annual rainfall. The same unit lets you compare the ocean with a catchment.

Take-home (bonus): exam-style question

Nitrate under a farm

⏱ at homeexam style
An unconfined sandstone aquifer lies under a farm. Area 4 km², saturated thickness 30 m, effective porosity 0.2. Rain recharges it at 250 mm/yr over its whole area. Nitrate fertiliser has leached into it for decades. Will stopping fertiliser use fix the problem quickly?
τ = amount ÷ flux     q = K · Δh / L     v = q / nₑ     t = distance / v
Constants: 1 km² = 10⁶ m²;  1 year = 365.25 days.
a)
How much water does the aquifer hold (m³)?
m³
💡 Area × saturated thickness × porosity.
Worked solution

Answer: 2.40×107 m³

4 × 10⁶ m² × 30 m × 0.2 = 2.4 × 10⁷ m³.
b)
How much recharge enters it each year (m³/yr)?
m³/yr
💡 Depth per year (m) × area (m²).
Worked solution

Answer: 1.00×106 m³/yr

0.250 m/yr × 4 × 10⁶ m² = 1.0 × 10⁶ m³/yr.
c)
What is the residence time of water in the aquifer (years)?
years
💡 τ = amount ÷ flux.
Worked solution

Answer: 24.0 years

2.4 × 10⁷ ÷ 1.0 × 10⁶ = 24 years.
d)
A supply borehole is 300 m down-gradient. The hydraulic gradient is 0.004 and K = 0.5 m/day. How long does water take to get there (years)?
years
💡 q = K × gradient; v = q / nₑ; t = distance ÷ v.
Worked solution

Answer: 82.1 years

q = 0.002 m/day; v = 0.01 m/day; t = 300 m ÷ 0.01 m/day = 30 000 days ≈ 82 years.
e)
The farmer stops using fertiliser today. Why might nitrate at the borehole keep rising for decades?
Model answer
Water (and its nitrate) takes decades to move through the aquifer: the residence time is ~24 years, and the water now arriving at the borehole entered up to ~82 years ago. Nitrate already in the unsaturated zone and the aquifer keeps arriving long after inputs stop — 'legacy nitrate', a real problem in UK chalk and sandstone aquifers.
Reading
Strongly recommended: Chapter 1 of Davie & Quinn (2019) Fundamentals of Hydrology (e-book via the library). Weil & Brady (2017) The Nature and Properties of Soils, sections 5.2–5.6 and 6.2–6.6. For C–Q: Li et al. (2024) Nature Climate Change 14, 225–237, and Knapp et al. (2020) Hydrology and Earth System Sciences 24, 2561–2576.
